newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish T-bill yields seen down, zloty battling NBP.
newsitem.headline: Polish T-bill yields seen down, zloty battling NBP.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields are likely to ease at the 1.3 billion zloty tender on Monday on high demand, with foreign bids keeping the zloty pitted against central bank-guarded levels throughout the week, dealers said.

They said demand at the tender was likely to total some 1.8 billion zlotys with domestic corporates and foreign speculators going for the 13-week paper and foreign portfolio investors buying the longer-term 26-week and 52-week bills.

"Demand at the tender might be some 1.6-1.8 billion zlotys. The shorter paper is likely to be sought by domestic firms and longer-term foreign investors are likely to bid for the 26-week and 52-week paper," said Robert Gluch of ING bank in Warsaw.
Dealers expected the maximum yield of the 52-week and 26-week bills to ease to 21.45 percent or more from around 21.50 percent at the last auction.

Dealers said such yields were still highly attractive for foreign investors despite no prospects of gains on the zloty's exchange rate, after the National Bank of Poland showed it was determined to keep the Polish currency from firming. @
The NBP has been consistently stepping in against the zloty whenever it rose above 2.5 percent from the centre of the daily trading band, buying dollars and marks.

"Next week might be very similar to this one, with the zloty battling against the 2.5 percent resistance and the NBP punching it down when it pokes its head above that level," said Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank in Warsaw.

Dealers said foreign players could be additionally drawn to zloty instruments after Friday's news that the new currency law, expected to be implemented in early 1998, would introduce external convertibility of the zloty. @

They also said Federal Reserve Alan Greenspan's remarks indicating that the next U.S. interest rates rise might be pushed back until July, could direct further capital into emerging markets, including Poland.

"The next U.S. interest rate rise might happen later rather than sooner, so some investors might be looking to park their capital here, especially after news that Poland's credit rating could be improved," one dealer at a foreign bank here said.
Earlier today, Standard and Poor's said that Poland's credit trend was fairly positive and that it would monitor the country's upcoming parliamentary elections closely. @
Currenty, Poland's foreign currency debt is rated BBB minus by S&P and Baa3 by Moody's Investors Service Inc.
